overview.description: Quatre Valets (Four Jacks), also widely known as Polignac or 'The Jacks Game', is a classic French trick-avoidance game. It is the direct ancestor to the modern Hearts family. Players compete to be the one taking the FEWEST Jacks in their captured tricks. The Jack of Spades (known as the Polignac) is the most heavily penalized card. It is a game of cautious leading, suit-bleeding, and protective play where every trick is a potential trap.

history.origins: Dates back to 18th-century France. Named after the Jules de Polignac, a key figure in the court of Louis XVI, reflecting the political rivalries of the era.
timeline: 1780s: First described as a social parlor game in Paris.
1880s: Standardized rules appear in Hoyle's manuals as 'The Jacks Game'.
Present: Still played globally as 'Polignac', serving as the'Purest' form of the trick-avoidance genre.
history.evolution: The game was simplified and the hearts-only penalty was later added by American players to create the game of 'Hearts'.
history.cultural: Used as a social metaphor for avoiding 'Unpleasant Associations'â€”the Jacks represent unwanted burdens.

setup.equipment: 32-card Piquet pack (French deck with 2s through 6s removed). For 3, 5, or 6 players remove the two black Sevens.
setup.dealing: Assign cards evenly. If playing with 3 or 5, remove extra cards to ensure an even deal.

rules.objective: Avoid taking tricks that contain Jacks. Achieve the lowest penalty score; the first player to reach the agreed penalty limit (e.g. 10 or 20 points) loses the game.
rules.gameplay: Eldest hand leads first. Players must follow suit if possible, otherwise may play any card. The trick is won by the highest card of the suit led; there are no trumps. The winner of each trick leads to the next. After all tricks are played, players incur penalties for each Jack captured: 2 points for the Jack of Spades (Polignac), 1 point for each other Jack. Rounds repeat until a player reaches the agreed penalty total and loses.
keyRules: Follow suit if possible; otherwise play any card.
No trumps. Trick won by highest card of the suit led.
Winner of each trick leads to the next.
Jack of Spades (Polignac) costs 2 penalty points; each other Jack costs 1.
First player to reach the agreed penalty total (e.g. 10 or 20) loses the game.

strategy.basic: Bleed the suits! If you hold a Jack, you must find a way to get rid of it. Lead your longest suit earlyâ€”this forces your opponents to follow suit, exhausting their safe cards. If you have a Jack and someone else leads that suit, play it ONLY if someone else has already played a higher card (like a King or Queen). This 'Dumping' of Jacks on others is the fundamental engine of the game.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Polignac' Protection: The Jack of Spades is your greatest enemy. If Spades are led, and you hold the King or Queen, you are in danger of winning the trick and capturing the Polignac. If you are the leader of a trick and you are void in Spades, lead a small card in a different suit to try and force a Spade lead later in the round from someone else.
strategy.advanced: Going for the 'General': If your hand is loaded with high cards (Kings and Aces) and you already have 2 Jacks, don't stop. Try to win EVERY trick that contains a Jack. If you secure all 4, you effectively win the round by penalty-reversal. However, if you miss even one Jack, you'll end up with the most points for the hand. This is the 'Moon-Shooting' of Quatre Valets.
tips: Keep track of which suits have had their 'Safety' removed (Aces and Kings are gone). Once the high cards are out, the Jacks become much more dangerous as leaders.
In a 4-player game, there are exactly 8 cards per suitâ€”memorize how many have been played!

list.name: Capot
list.description: Before the opening lead, any player may bid capot (undertaking to win every trick). If they succeed, each opponent loses 5 penalty points; if they fail, the bidder loses 5.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Capot changes only round scoring; no engine constant overrides identified yet.

list.name: General
list.description: Before leading to the first trick, a player may announce they are going for the general (taking all tricks). If they succeed, all other players score 5 penalty points each; if they fail, the Jacks score 5 penalty points each against the players who take them.
list.emptyOverridesReason: General changes only round scoring; no engine constant overrides identified yet.

list.name: Ace high variant
list.description: If players prefer Ace to rank high (common in old French games), penalties attach to Queens instead of Jacks.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Ace high shifts penalty cards to Queens; no engine overrides documented yet.

difficulty.easy: Wins tricks accidentally; holds Jacks until the very end; poor suit tracking.
difficulty.medium: Dumps Jacks when void; protects against Polignac; understands the 'General' risk.
difficulty.hard: Expert at 'Suit Exhaustion'; perfectly times 'General' attempts; manipulates turns to force opponents to lead their Jacks.

phases.label: Deal
phases.notes: Dealer deals all cards evenly (8 each for 4 players; with 3, 5, or 6 players remove two black Sevens and deal evenly).

phases.label: Play
phases.notes: Eldest leads first; follow suit if possible. Trick won by highest of led suit; winner leads next. Eight tricks per round.

phases.label: Score round
phases.notes: Assign penalties for Jacks taken; if no one reached agreed limit, next round (deal); else game over.

engine.deckDescription: A stripped French deck containing 32 cards with four suits (Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, Spades) and eight ranks per suit (7 through Ace), created by removing all 2s through 6s from a standard 52-card deck for trick-taking play.
engine.suitDescription: Four traditional French suits: Hearts (Cœur), Diamonds (Carreau), Clubs (Trèfle), and Spades (Pique), each represented with standard French card design and color coding for easy suit identification and trick determination.
engine.rankDescription: Eight ranks per suit in ascending order: 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack (Valet), Queen (Dame), King (Roi), and Ace as the highest card, where Jacks carry special penalty significance in this trick-taking game.
engine.dealPattern: All cards dealt evenly in one pass (8 each for 4 players; with 3, 5, or 6 players remove two cards and deal evenly).
